title: Consent as Nonverbal Negotiation
hook: Bodies negotiate consent all the time, by leaning in, pulling back and going still, but only a clear yes, freely given and still present, counts as one.
why:
Every touch between two people involves a quiet negotiation. A hand reaches out, and the other person leans in or draws back. A hug begins, and the other body softens or stiffens. In play, in comfort, in sex, bodies constantly signal willingness and reluctance, and most of the time people read each other well enough. The chapter on touch in Part I set out the hard line this book keeps: touch is the one channel where you must ask, and only a clear yes grants permission.

This chapter takes that line further. It explains why refusals are usually indirect and why that does not excuse misunderstanding; what research shows about how men and women signal and read consent; why stillness and silence are never a yes; how drink, fear and power remove the freedom and capacity to agree; how to ask and keep checking; and how the same principles apply to hugs, play and children. It teaches reading in order to stop and ask, never in order to proceed.

teach.p:
Watch any physical interaction between two people and you will see a continuous exchange. One person moves closer; the other matches the move or holds still or steps back. A hand rests on an arm; the arm relaxes under it or slides away. An embrace starts; the other body meets it, endures it or pulls out of it. This happens in a hug between friends, in rough play between brothers, in a haircut, in a medical examination and in sex.

Reading these signals is a basic skill, and most people do it constantly without noticing. A friend who stiffens when you put an arm around him is read, and the arm comes away. A child who squirms out of a hug is let go. Much of the time, the negotiation works.

But reading is not the same as agreeing, and this chapter turns on that difference. The body can tell you to stop. It cannot, on its own, tell you that you may go on. Signs of willingness are easily misread, as the previous chapter showed, while signs of reluctance, once noticed, are reason enough to stop. The asymmetry is the whole point: read the body for no, and ask for yes.

The figures here show one person leaning in and the other leaning back, arms folded, turning away. In any physical situation, this is the body saying stop. Whatever has been said or done before, the right response is to step back and, if it matters, to ask.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if signs of willingness could be read as reliably as signs of reluctance. The research on overperception in the previous chapter suggests they cannot, which is why the body should be read for no and asked for yes.
teach.pullQuote: Read the body for no, and ask for yes.

teach.p:
A common defence of sexual misconduct is miscommunication: she never actually said no. In 1999 Celia Kitzinger and Hannah Frith took that defence apart using the methods of conversation analysis. In ordinary life, they pointed out, people almost never refuse anything with a bare no. They decline invitations with delays, hesitations, hedges, apologies and excuses: “Well, um, I'd love to, but I'm really tired.” Everyone understands these as refusals, and nobody treats a dinner invitation declined this way as accepted.

Kitzinger and Frith argued that sexual refusals follow the same patterns, and that a man who claims not to understand a refusal because it did not include the word no is claiming an ignorance that he does not show anywhere else in his life. In 2006 Rachael O'Byrne, Mark Rapley and Susan Hansen tested this with focus groups of young men, and found that the men readily understood subtle and nonverbal refusals, describing them in detail, even as they sometimes argued that women should simply say no.

The lesson is plain. You already know how to hear a refusal. Hesitation, delay, an excuse, a change of subject, a body that turns away or goes rigid: these are refusals, and you understand them in every other setting.

The figure here has turned away. In a conversation, you would know at once that it was over. The same knowledge applies in every physical situation, and the absence of the word no does not change it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people generally refused things with a direct no, or if indirect refusals were commonly misunderstood. Conversation research shows that refusals are typically indirect and understood, though the studies of young men were small and qualitative.

teach.h: Men lean on the body more.
teach.p:
In a survey of 185 university students published in 2014, Kristen Jozkowski and her colleagues asked how people communicated and interpreted consent to sex. Women reported using more verbal ways of signalling consent; men reported more nonverbal ones. And when interpreting a partner's consent or refusal, men relied more on nonverbal signals than women did. Many students defined consent as an explicit agreement, yet described relying on signals that were much less clear than that.

Put that alongside the previous chapter and a risk appears. Men tend to overestimate sexual interest, and men tend to rely on the body to judge consent. A man who reads a partner's body generously, and does not ask, is relying on exactly the kind of judgment that is most likely to be wrong.

This is not a claim that men are bad at reading or that nonverbal signals are worthless. Most of the time, between partners who know each other, bodies communicate well. It is a claim about where errors come from and what corrects them. Words correct them. A simple question costs nothing between people who want the same thing, and protects everyone when they do not.

The figure here sits turned toward someone, engaged. Engagement in a conversation is not agreement to anything else, and a body that seems willing is still worth asking.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men and women relied equally on verbal and nonverbal signals of consent. Jozkowski and colleagues found a difference, though in one university sample and through self-report, so the size of the difference elsewhere is uncertain.

teach.p:
The chapter on trauma in Part II described tonic immobility: the involuntary freezing that can happen when escape seems impossible. In a study of women who came to an emergency clinic after sexual assault, Anna Möller and her colleagues found that most reported significant immobility during the assault. They did not fight, scream or say no, because their bodies would not let them.

Freezing is the most extreme form of a wider truth. People go still for many reasons other than willingness: fear, shock, confusion, a sense that resisting would make things worse, dissociation, or simply not knowing how to stop something without causing a scene. Some people go along with touch they do not want because they fear the consequences of refusing, especially from someone bigger, older, more powerful or more insistent.

So treat stillness, silence and passivity as signs to stop, never as signs to continue. A partner who stops responding, goes limp or rigid, turns their face away, stops returning touch or seems to be somewhere else is telling you something, and the response is to pause and ask: “Are you okay? Do you want to stop?” If the answer is anything other than a clear yes to continuing, stop.

The figure here stands frozen, arms tight to the body. In a dangerous street, this is fear. In any physical situation between two people, it means that whatever is happening should stop at once.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people who did not want touch always resisted it actively. Research on tonic immobility and on why people go along with unwanted touch shows that many do not, which is why stillness can never be read as agreement.

teach.p:
A yes counts only when it is free and when the person giving it is able to give it. The law in England and Wales puts it in a single sentence: a person consents if they agree by choice, and have the freedom and capacity to make that choice. Other places use different words, but the principles are widely shared.

Capacity can be lost long before someone passes out. The courts in England have recognised that a person can be too intoxicated to make a choice while still appearing conscious. The chapter on substance use in Part II described the signs of heavy intoxication: slurred speech, unsteadiness, confusion, eyes that do not focus, difficulty following a conversation. Someone showing these signs cannot meaningfully agree to sex, whatever they say, and someone who has been drinking heavily himself is in no state to judge.

Freedom can be removed by fear, pressure, threats, persistence, dependence or power. A yes extracted after repeated asking, given to a boss, a landlord, a coach or someone much bigger, or given because saying no felt dangerous, is not a free choice. The chapters on touch and greetings described how power makes refusal harder. In intimate situations it does so even more.

The figure here stands slumped, unsteady. If someone you are with looks like this, the only question is how to get them safely home, with their friends or with help. Nothing else is on the table.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if intoxication, fear or pressure left a person's agreement as meaningful as when they were sober and free. Legal definitions of consent in many places, and the research on coercion, treat freedom and capacity as essential.

teach.p:
Asking does not have to be clumsy, and it does not spoil anything. “Is this okay?” “Do you want to?” “Do you want me to stop?” Said warmly, at the right moment, these questions are part of intimacy, not an interruption to it. Many people say that being asked makes them feel safer and more willing, not less.

Consent is not a single gate passed once. People can agree to one thing and not another, agree and then change their minds, or agree last week and not tonight. So keep checking as things change, especially when moving to something new, and especially when the other person's body changes: when they go quiet, stop returning touch, tense up or pull back.

Make stopping easy. Say it out loud: “We can stop any time.” If they hesitate, stop and give them room, rather than waiting to see whether the hesitation passes. Look for active participation, not mere absence of objection: if someone is not taking an active part, stop and ask. And when someone says no, or not now, accept it without sulking, arguing or trying again later the same night. The way you take a no tells the other person whether it is safe to say one.

The figures here stand at an angle, close enough to speak, far enough that either can step away. A good question about touch is asked from somewhere like this, where both people are free to say no.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if asking about consent made intimate encounters worse for those involved. Accounts from people who are asked suggest the opposite, though formal research on this question is limited.

teach.h: Consent everywhere: hugs, play and children.
teach.p:
Consent is not only about sex. Everything in this chapter applies to a hug, a play fight, a hand on the shoulder or tickling a child. The previous chapters on hugs and touch between friends described offering touch in a way that can be declined and stopping as soon as the body says no. The same rules apply to the people with least power to refuse.

Children are the clearest case. A child who is tickled will often laugh while saying stop, because tickling causes laughter whether or not it is enjoyed. Stop when they say stop, every time, and they learn that their no works. A child who is told to hug or kiss a relative they do not want to touch learns that their body belongs to whoever is asking. Offer alternatives, such as a wave or a high five, and let them choose. The chapter on fatherhood returns to this.

And if you have been on the receiving end of touch you did not want, as many men have, or you are worried that you have done harm to someone, specialist help exists. In the United States, the RAINN National Sexual Assault Hotline is on 800-656-4673. In England and Wales, the Rape Crisis support line is on 0808 500 2222. Other countries have their own services, and the crisis resources in this app list general lines for anyone in distress.

The figures here show an adult down at a child's height. Asking a child whether they want a hug, and accepting no, is where everything in this chapter begins.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if children who were made to accept unwanted touch learned nothing from it. The claim is supported by child-protection guidance rather than by controlled research, and should be read as a widely shared principle.

poseGallery.doCaption: Asking first, with room to say no
poseGallery.annotation: The body can tell you to stop, but not that you may go on. Ask in words, from a distance that leaves the other person free.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Carrying on when someone goes still
poseGallery.annotation: Stillness, silence and a body that stops responding all mean stop. Pause and ask; continue only on a clear yes.

poseGallery.dontCaption: A hug a child did not choose
poseGallery.annotation: Children learn whether their no works from the adults around them. Offer a wave or a high five as an alternative, and let them choose.

caseStudy:
Ollie, twenty-four, is at a house party when he notices his friend Jake steering a woman toward the stairs. Ollie does not know her. She is stumbling, holding the banister with both hands, her eyes not quite focusing, and she does not seem to be answering when Jake talks to her.

Ollie's first instinct is that it is none of his business. Then he remembers a session at work on bystander intervention, and the three options it described: distract, delegate or deal with it directly. He goes over and says to Jake, cheerfully, that someone is asking for him outside about his car. While Jake hesitates, Ollie asks the woman if she is all right and whether her friends are here. She mumbles a name. Ollie finds the friend, who is horrified and takes her to a quiet room with water.

Jake is angry. He tells Ollie she was up for it. Ollie says, quietly, that she could not stand up, and that he would rather Jake was annoyed with him than in a police station, or worse, that she was hurt. Jake leaves the party.

The next morning Jake messages. He says he was drunk, that he did not see how bad she was, and that he feels sick thinking about it. Ollie replies that he gets it, and that the drink was part of the problem for both of them.

It changes something for Ollie too. With his girlfriend, he starts saying what he had always assumed: “Is this okay?” He is surprised by how much she likes being asked, and by how much easier it makes everything.
observe: Notice everyday refusals around you: invitations declined, offers turned down. How many use the word no?
Notice how people's bodies signal reluctance to touch: a stiffened hug, a hand withdrawn, a step back.
Notice how you respond when someone declines your touch, even a handshake or a hug, and what your response teaches them.
Notice how adults around you respond when a child says stop during play.

drills.name: Hear the Refusal
steps: Write down five ways people declined invitations from you in the past month.
Note how many used the word no, and what words and signals they used instead.
Write down how you understood each one, and whether you were ever in doubt.
Write one sentence about what this tells you about refusals in intimate situations.

drills.name: Words for Checking
steps: Write five short, warm ways of asking whether someone wants to continue.
Say each aloud until it sounds natural in your voice.
Write a response for no and not now that is gracious and contains no pressure.
Choose the two you are most likely to use.

drills.name: Capacity Check
steps: Write down the signs of heavy intoxication from the chapter on substance use.
Write a personal rule for what you will do if someone you are with shows them.
Write down how you would help a stranger in that state, using distract, delegate or direct.
Look up the emergency number and a sexual assault support line where you live, and save them.

drills.name: A Child's No
steps: If you have children in your life, notice one moment this week when a child says stop or pulls away during play or affection.
Stop at once, and say something simple, such as “Okay, I've stopped.”
Offer a choice the next time you greet them: a hug, a high five or a wave.
Notice how the child responds over the following weeks.

quiz.q: Someone says that if a person does not say no, it is fair to assume they agree. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since anyone who does not want something will say so
Refusals are usually indirect, and stillness is never a yes
He is right as long as the person has not pulled away physically
Silence counts as a yes once two people are in a relationship
quiz.explain: Kitzinger and Frith showed that people rarely refuse anything with a bare no, and that indirect refusals are understood in everyday life. Freezing, silence and passivity can reflect fear or shock, so only a clear, free yes counts.

quiz.q: What did Kitzinger and Frith conclude about how people refuse?
options: People nearly always refuse with a clear and direct no
Refusals are hard to understand unless the word no is used
Refusals usually come with delays and excuses, and are understood
Indirect refusals are understood by women but never by men
quiz.explain: Ordinary refusals come wrapped in hesitation, hedges and excuses, and everyone understands them as refusals. O'Byrne and colleagues found that young men readily understood subtle and nonverbal refusals too.

quiz.q: What did Jozkowski and colleagues find about how students judged a partner's consent?
options: Men relied more than women on nonverbal signals to judge consent
Women relied entirely on nonverbal signals and never asked at all
Both men and women always asked directly before any intimacy
Students were unable to say how they judged consent at all
quiz.explain: Men reported relying more on nonverbal signals to interpret consent, and women used more verbal ways of signalling it. Combined with men's tendency to overestimate interest, this is a reason to ask rather than read.

quiz.q: Under the law in England and Wales, when does a person consent?
options: Whenever they have not physically resisted what is happening
Once they have said yes at any point earlier in the evening
When they are conscious, whatever their level of intoxication
When they agree by choice, with the freedom and capacity to choose
quiz.explain: The law defines consent as agreeing by choice with the freedom and capacity to make that choice. Courts have recognised that capacity can be lost through intoxication before a person becomes unconscious.

quiz.q: During an intimate moment, your partner goes quiet, stops responding and turns their face away. What should you do?
options: Carry on gently, since they have not actually said that they want you to stop
Pause, ask whether they are okay, and stop unless they clearly say yes
Speed up, so that the moment does not lose its momentum
Ask them to explain exactly what is wrong before you will stop
quiz.explain: A body that stops responding is a reason to stop and check. Continue only on a clear yes, and accept anything else without pressure.

quiz.q: A young child is laughing while you tickle him, but he keeps saying stop. What fits this chapter best?
options: Keep going, since the laughter shows he is really enjoying it
Slow down a little, but carry on until he stops laughing
Stop at once, so that he learns his no is always respected
Ask his mother whether he really means it before you stop
quiz.explain: Tickling causes laughter whether or not it is enjoyed. Stopping when a child says stop teaches him that his no works, which is the foundation of consent.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific moment when you were not sure whether someone wanted to be touched: a hug, play, comfort or intimacy. Describe the signals you noticed, what you did, and how you know, or do not know, what they wanted. Then think of a moment when someone touched you in a way you did not want. How did your body respond, and did you say anything? What would asking, and being asked, have changed in each case?
reflection.guidance: This reflection may bring up uncomfortable memories, on either side. Write only what you are comfortable writing. If it brings up something that distresses you, the support lines in this chapter and the crisis resources in the app are there. The aim is not to judge yourself but to notice how often reading was doing the work that asking should have done.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat the absence of a no as a yes, when refusals are usually indirect and understood in every other setting. The second is to read stillness, silence or passivity as agreement, when they can mean fear, shock or freezing. The third is to rely on the body to judge willingness, when men in particular tend to overread interest and to lean on nonverbal signals. The fourth is to ignore capacity and freedom: someone who is heavily intoxicated, frightened or under pressure cannot freely agree. And the fifth is to forget that consent applies everywhere, to hugs, play and children as much as to sex. Read the body for no, ask for yes, and keep checking.

watch.title: Tea and Consent
watch.notice: The well-known animation comparing consent to offering a cup of tea. Notice the points about people who are asleep, who change their minds, or who said yes last time: consent has to be present, ongoing and freely given.

reviewPrompt: This week, notice three everyday refusals that did not use the word no, and practise one warm way of asking whether someone wants to continue.
